mustKnowNow.meaning: A debate round is two sides arguing opposite answers to one statement (the motion) in front of a judge, and the judge picks the side whose reasons held up best based only on what was said in the round, so your job is not just to talk: it is to leave your reasons still standing at the end.

A round is not a list of speeches; it is a handful of arguments that keep changing - each one gets introduced, then answered or ignored, then defended or dropped - and nothing resets when a new speaker stands up.
Every time a speech ends, ask two separate questions about each argument: was it answered, yes or no - and what state is it in now?

An argument can be in one of three states - still unresolved (it was answered, but the answer did not settle it), weakened (answered and never defended), or sitting exactly where it was made (no response at all) - so after every opposing speech, defend the ones that were answered.

If the other side never answers one of your arguments they have not beaten it - it is still there in the shape you gave it, it can decide a round you thought you were winning, and pointing that out costs one sentence.
While the other side is speaking, listen instead of rehearsing: catch each of their claims and the reason under it, and mark which of your own arguments they answered and which they skipped.

Early speeches mostly build your side's case and later ones mostly answer and compare, so the round narrows to a few arguments still in dispute - and the judge decides between those survivors, not between who said more or who sounded surer.

mustKnowNow.meaning: Every argument you make has three parts — a claim (the exact thing you want the judge to agree with, specific enough to argue about), a warrant (why it is true), and an impact (why it matters) — and the judge weighs all three.
The warrant is a mechanism: name the cause-and-effect step that makes the claim true — how the thing you want actually produces the result you claim.

A warrant fails in two ways — it repeats the claim in different words, or it names the problem without naming the cause — so finish '...because ___' with a cause-and-effect step, not a synonym, and check your draft: if every sentence could stand on its own as an assertion, the reasoning is still missing.

The impact answers the judge's silent 'so what?' — say who is affected, how badly, and how many — because 'it helps everyone' gives the judge nothing to weigh, and an argument that is true but has no impact still loses.

A fact or a source name is not an argument: the judge has to stay neutral and will not connect it for you, and the same fact usually fits both sides — so you say the connecting sentence out loud, 'which means ___, therefore ___.'
Making an argument stronger means improving the warrant and the impact — the claim stays exactly the same — and you get there by revising in passes, not by saying the claim more forcefully.

mustKnowNow.meaning: Evidence gives the judge a reason to believe a claim; it does not automatically prove it. You are judging how far that reason reaches.
Start from the claim, not the evidence: say in one sentence what would have to be shown for the claim to hold.
Say what the evidence actually shows: what was measured or observed, in whom, over what period, compared with what.

Check the fit: evidence about something nearby is not evidence about the claim. Sign-ups are not results, intentions are not behaviour, liking the gym is not fitness. A real, expert, trustworthy source can still be answering the wrong question.
Check the size: evidence from one case, one place, or one group supports a claim about that case. A claim about many needs many. Evidence that covers part of a claim leaves the rest still a claim.
Two things happening together, or one happening after the other, is not one causing the other until the other explanations are dealt with.
Grant and gap: take the evidence as true, say what it does establish, name what is still unproven, and shrink the claim to fit what is left.

safetyBoundaries.meaning: B01 — the evidence/claim link is the 'warrant'; name the noun once, never teach how to build one
B02 — how to SAY the reasoning belongs to the Claim, Warrant, Impact lesson; this lesson only judges support
B03 — you judge the evidence as described, taking it as true; you need not disprove it and need not look anything up
B04 — one case supports a claim about that case; it USUALLY cannot, BY ITSELF, justify a broad claim about many cases
B05 — a comparison group rules out ONLY the explanations both groups share, so it makes the tested cause the likeliest explanation, not a proven one
B06 — a conflict of interest is a reason for extra scrutiny of how a result was produced, not a reason to throw the result away
B07 — when the method cannot be examined, that LIMITS confidence next to a result whose method is open; it does not turn the evidence into an assertion and is not grounds for rejection

B08 — repeating the same underlying source does not create independent corroboration; three articles citing one survey are one survey, though a single source can still contain several distinct findings

mustKnowNow.meaning: A judge is holding several arguments apart at once and writes your answer wherever you point it, so signposting means saying which argument you are on before you argue.
Before every answer, say the argument it is answering, and say it again each time you move to a new one.
Name the argument itself, in whatever words you like and never by its number or its speaker, then use a recognisable version of that same name every time you come back to it.
In a speech that answers the other side, open by saying what answers are coming and what each one is on, in the order you will take them.

What a side says comes in sizes — a broad AREA, the ARGUMENTS inside it, and the INNER CLAIMS each argument rests on, at whatever size the other side actually built them — so name the piece your answer is really about.

safetyBoundaries.meaning: B01. A roadmap that gives a count but no argument names is still a roadmap, only a weaker one. The rule must never be stated as requiring both a count and names.
B02. A sentence stating your position or your conclusion is not a roadmap, however confident it sounds — it describes what you intend to prove, not the shape of the speech.

mustKnowNow.meaning: An argument is a conclusion held up by supports. Refuting means taking one support away and saying what the conclusion has lost — not saying you disagree with it.

Before you speak, grant your own answer: if the judge accepted everything you are about to say, could the other side still make their argument in the same words and reach the same conclusion? If yes, you have not refuted anything.

Aim at a support that is BOTH necessary (their conclusion cannot be reached without it) and contestable (you can actually give the judge a reason to doubt it). Being right about a detail their argument does not need changes nothing.
A finished answer has four parts: "They say ___, but ___ because ___. Therefore ___." Most beginners stop after the first two.

The because has to name something the other side could argue back at — a mechanism, a condition, a mismatch, a step that does not follow. Test it: cover the words after "because" and reread; if the answer means the same thing without them, they explained nothing.
Finish by saying what their argument can no longer establish — and stop there. Do not turn to your own case.

safetyBoundaries.meaning: Report the argument you actually damaged, not the case. Taking out one support inside one argument is not the collapse of their case; claiming it is claims ground you did not take.
"Support" is Refutation's word for EVERY load-bearing part of an argument, any of which can be answered. It must not be renamed or narrowed.

The productive attempt stays a constructed four-slot answer on the exact frame "They say ___, but ___ because ___. Therefore ___." with slots ["they say","but","because","therefore"], set against an authored opponentClaim that is a CLAIM and carries no reasoning.

mustKnowNow.meaning: Before you judge an answer, ask two questions in this order: if this answer worked perfectly, what would be true in the round? (that gives you the direction) and only then, what did the answer go after? (that gives you the name).

Every answer points one of two ways: DEFENSE makes their argument count for less (smaller, shakier, or gone) and adds nothing new for your side, while OFFENSE gives the judge a reason to prefer your side that was not there before.

Each direction holds one named move — an INDICT is defense aimed at the evidence itself (who produced it, what it measured, how the result was reached), a TURN is offense in which their own argument is what supplies your reason — and an answer that is neither simply keeps its direction's name: plain defense, or offense that is a reason of your own standing beside their argument.

How hard your answer hits and how good your evidence is do not set the direction — you can destroy their argument completely and still have only defense, and the same strong study is defense if it finds their effect is not there but a turn if it finds the effect runs the other way.

Defense is a real answer and often the right one, but choose it on purpose: judges vote for reasons, so if every answer you make is defense and their argument is still standing, the judge is left holding their reason and none of yours.

The four names also run backwards: look at the argument in front of you, ask what needs to change about it — does it need to count for less, or does something need to start counting for you — and pick the direction from that answer.

safetyBoundaries.meaning: One answer often does more than one thing at once — a reversal usually stops their argument helping them AND gives you a reason — and the two-way sort is a classification by the reason the answer creates, not a claim that an answer has only one effect.

Aiming at their evidence does not by itself make an indict. An indict is the DEFENSIVE evidence-aimed answer; if what you show about their evidence makes their own argument point your way, what you have is a turn.

More than one direction is often available on the same argument — but a direction the argument's own terms do not support is never available: you cannot reverse an argument that never points your way.

Classifying correctly is not refuting. "This is a turn" describes what your answer would accomplish and is not a reason for the judge to accept it — the reason and the loss to their argument still have to be said out loud.

Refutation's vocabulary is broader: it calls every load-bearing part of an argument a support, and any of them can be answered. Denying a step in their reasoning is a real answer and often good defense — it is just not an indict.

Classification is success-conditional: you class an answer by what it would establish IF it were accepted, not by whether it lands. Either answer can still fail, and a turn is a turn whether or not the judge ends up believing it.

mustKnowNow.meaning: An argument that predicts something bad has three parts: the ACTION (what we would do), the LINK (what they say that causes), and the IMPACT (why they say that outcome is bad). If it arrives as one clause, split it with three questions.

Four of the choices have names: deny the connection = NO-LINK (defense), reverse the connection = LINK TURN (offense), shrink the endpoint = IMPACT DEFENSE (defense), reverse the endpoint = IMPACT TURN (offense) — four different moves, not four strengths of one move.
To tell which move you made, ask what would be true if your answer completely succeeded: does that part disappear, get smaller, or point the other way?
A reversal only counts for your side if the reversed result depends on your side winning — if it would happen anyway, you have not turned anything.
Two of your own answers, granted together, can add up to a reason to vote AGAINST your side — that is a DOUBLE TURN, and the problem is what the pair adds up to, never how many reversals you made.

Before you speak, check any pair you plan to run together: say what outcome each answer is about, ask whether that is the same thing, then grant both and ask whether YOUR side is now the thing that removes the good, or delivers the harm, your other answer just named — if it is, keep the reversal you can win and let the other part take plain defense or silence.

safetyBoundaries.meaning: B01 — shrinking splits into 'less of the outcome arrives' (a claim about how strongly the connection works) and 'the outcome arrives but matters less', which is the one called IMPACT DEFENSE; none of it is weighing.
B02 — a double turn does NOT require the two claims to be incompatible; they usually can both be true, and that is exactly why the opponent can agree with both and take the ballot.

B03 — 'the same outcome' means the same on FOUR counts, conjunctively: same measure, same who or what in the same place, same stretch of time, same conditions. Never a disjunction, never 'the same people'.
B04 — two reversals about genuinely different outcomes sit together perfectly well; reversals that look like a pair may not be one.
B05 — answers to two DIFFERENT arguments can collide when they meet on one outcome; the collision is not confined to a single chain.
B06 — the offense test is success-conditional: what the answer would establish if accepted, not whether the judge ends up believing it.
B07 — a reversal that fails the depends-on-your-side test has not earned the name at all, so Answer Types' rule that a turn is always offense still holds.
B08 — naming the move says what you are trying to accomplish; building it into a complete answer with the because and the therefore is the REFUTATION lesson's job, not this one's.
B09 — a reason of your own that does not run through their argument is offense but NOT a turn; a turn takes their outcome and makes it yours.
B10 — an answer aimed at their evidence is an indict, which is DEFENSE; it becomes a turn only when what you show makes their own argument point your way.

B11 — the labels travel with the idea, not with every format: Public Forum uses them, many parliamentary judges call all of it refutation, and if the vocabulary draws blank looks you drop the labels and keep the logic.

mustKnowNow.meaning: Your CASE is everything your side argues in the round. A CONTENTION is one big point inside it, with the arguing underneath. A constructive is a few contentions put together as one case — not a list of every argument you own.

The first constructive is where you put your OWN side's case up. There is usually nothing to answer yet, so a speech that spends its time answering arguments the other side has not made hands the judge their case first and leaves yours half-built.
A contention goes first if a later one only works once the judge has accepted it. Choose the order from what depends on what — not from which point feels strongest or which you wrote first.
Every contention has to do a job none of the others does. Two contentions that establish the same thing look like two parts and are really one.
A contention counts only when you actually argue it. Announcing the heading, or naming a claim, a warrant and a source somewhere in that stretch, is not the same as having argued it.
Finish by saying what your contentions show together. Do not say you have already beaten the other side's case — it has not been made yet, so there is nothing there to beat.

safetyBoundaries.meaning: Claim/warrant/impact is IMPORTED here in exactly one sentence and is NOT owned by this lesson. Do not expand it, exemplify it, or re-teach it — Constructive owns whole-speech composition.

Arguments you never establish in the constructive are hard to revive later.

mustKnowNow.meaning: Weighing means putting both impacts side by side and telling the judge which one should decide the round; saying more about your own harm is not weighing.
Give the judge a rule for choosing — a weighing standard, also called a weighing framework — and word it so it could be used on either side's impact, not just yours.

Build the rule on a difference these two harms really have, and say why that difference should decide — a rule both sides come out the same under settles nothing, and a difference with no reason attached is only a fact.
Say your rule early, while there are still speeches left in which the other side can answer it — and expect them to argue for a different rule.
Run both impacts through your rule and say what it decides — stating the rule is not the same as making the comparison.
When a real difference runs their way, name it, then argue why the difference you are standing on should still control — naming both and stopping is not weighing.

safetyBoundaries.meaning: Magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility are names for common comparison moves, never required speech vocabulary — the skill is making the comparison clear, not saying the lens words, and there is no ranking of comparisons to memorise.
Do not present the round as though every comparison favours you — a judge who can see the difference you skipped trusts the ones you made less.

Timing is a separate axis from content: the same words are strong or weak depending only on which speech the rule arrives in, and the fix for a late rule is to have given it in an earlier speech, not to reorder the final one.
Frames and scaffolds are optional structure, never required wording — filling in a blank does not make what you put in it true, and naming a kind of comparison is not the same as making one.
